XVII is a sixteen-track audio studio in Rust and Dioxus, designed for annotating my metal songs: laying down a structure (verse, riff A, breakdown, solo), setting a tempo that changes along the way, and synchronising lyrics line by line and then word by word. The name comes from the Roman numeral seventeen: the seventeenth track, the one for lyrics, which is added to the sixteen audio tracks.

As of 26 October 2026, only phase 1 of the roadmap's 6 has been delivered: playing an audio file passed as an argument in a minimal window, with an adjustable master gain. The full architecture, though, was settled in writing before the first line of code.

## The problem

My songs do not follow a tidy verse-chorus structure: blast beats, half-time and double-time, breaks that never return in the same form. Common automatic annotation tools assume a regular structure and get this kind of music wrong, or worse, impose their reading without saying so. I wanted a tool that proposes an analysis when it can, but never takes control away from me: laying down a section, correcting a tempo, resynchronising a line must always remain possible, whatever the quality of the automatic detection.

The second problem is personal. I am comfortable in Rust but a complete beginner in signal processing. XVII is as much a tool I want to use as a project for learning real-time audio programming and the basics of DSP (FFT, transient detection, tempo estimation) before tackling the part that interests me most.

The real architecture problem, then, is this: how do you build an audio engine whose real-time thread tolerates no pause, while letting a human interface and, tomorrow, an AI assistant drive the same application without ever duplicating the validation rules?

## The technical decisions

**The model knows neither audio nor the interface.** The `xvii-model` crate depends only on `serde`: it is Cargo, not a convention, that forbids bringing an audio or UI type into it. Above it, `xvii-engine` and `xvii-decode` know only the model; `xvii-app` (Dioxus) and `xvii-mcp` (the future server for an AI assistant) are the only two assembly points, and they do not know each other. Both will go through the same door, `EngineHandle`, where a gain is bounded to ×1.5 and a seek to 2^60 frames: validation lives once, not once per consumer.

**The audio thread obeys six non-negotiable rules, with no exceptions.** The `cpal` callback must never allocate or free memory, never take a lock, never perform I/O, and must run in bounded time; all communication goes through a lock-free queue (`rtrb`, one producer, one consumer) and atomics. The subtlest rule: never release an `Arc` on this thread. Replacing a track sends the old one to a return queue that the interface empties at its leisure, with a last resort if it overflows: leak the memory (`mem::forget`) rather than break the rule. `xvii-engine/src/rt.rs` (486 lines) concentrates this code, covered by 12 tests that run without a sound card, since CI machines have none.

**A volume change must never be abrupt.** Applying a gain instantly produces an audible click ("zipper noise"): the waveform jumps like a staircase step. Track, mute and master gains therefore glide towards their target value through a one-pole exponential filter with a time constant of about 5 ms, short enough to react, long enough that no ear can hear it.

**All analysis data must stay editable by hand, with its provenance and its confidence.** This is decision D11: nothing produced by the future analysis module will be final; a detected section will carry a confidence and can be overwritten by a section laid down by hand, which always prevails. This is not an abstract precaution: on a passage of distorted vocals (growl, scream), speech recognition loses the phonemes and its confidence collapses, and the interface brief already provides for a visual state of "visible give-up" rather than inventing a result. I prefer a tool that says it does not know to one that lies politely.

**A critical review of the code found five real bugs before they became audible.** An extreme seek made the playhead's arithmetic panic; a device advertising up to 34 channels ("pro audio" mode) could be chosen by default although the mixer feeds only two; a quick double press on play/pause could swallow the second press; playback did not pause at the end of the file; a device error was never reported to the interface. All five were fixed in the same commit, with the seek bound brought back to a single validation point.

## What I learned from it

That documenting an architecture before writing code forces you to settle questions (which internal time unit, who is allowed to modify what) that you would otherwise put off until later, when they cost the most to fix. That real-time audio is a discipline of its own: most of the reflexes of "normal" programming (allocating, locking, performing I/O) are forbidden there, and you need a different vocabulary (lock-free queues, atomics, return queue) to do without them. And that setting a rule like D11 at design time avoids discovering after the fact that automatic detection will fail on my own music.

What I would do differently: not leave the project paused for several months right after the scaffolding, and aim for a shorter vertical slice that reaches the DSP part in the very first sessions, rather than delivering all the plumbing (workspace, decoding, minimal window) before tackling it. That is precisely the part that interested me most when I started, and it is the one I have not yet begun.

Vefta is the personal productivity suite I am building for Kovelt SAS, the company I founded and where I am the sole developer. Until July 2026 it was called Chronos. The starting idea: a single tool that holds a person's calendar, tasks, contacts, notes, mail and messaging, that works without a connection and whose data never leaves the user's control.

The native foundation and two-way synchronisation with Google Calendar have been delivered since June 2026 (MVP1). The mail cell is being tested by alpha testers. Unified messaging is designed and documented, but not yet built. The professional back office for organisations (Teams) follows the same principle, but its construction remains explicitly frozen behind a measurable economic trigger: that an independent user prefers Vefta to Google and pays the subscription. On-device AI is treated differently: it is a long-term workstream already under way, with fine-tuning of the small local language model in progress. It is free because it runs on the user's own device at almost zero marginal cost, unlike cloud AI, which will remain paid.

## The problem

The starting observation is a concrete one: a freelance graphic designer who always has five tabs open (calendar, mail, notes, a translator and invoicing) and whose tools know nothing about one another. Her address book knows nothing of her appointment history, her calendar knows nothing of her mail, and the whole lot lives with vendors whose business model rests on exploiting her data.

Three concrete frictions follow. Fragmentation: the same information about the same person is scattered across silos that do not talk to each other. Dependence: the dominant suites impose their own account as the user's identity, make leaving costly and fund their free tier with targeted advertising. No local grounding: no major player really models France, with public holidays by zone, school holidays by académie, the tax calendar, and administrative services such as Ameli or the CAF.

Vefta answers each of these frictions with a technical stance rather than a commercial one: a single application rather than a set of walled-off tools, a client that works without the cloud and exportable data rather than a captive account, and French public calendars layered in natively rather than ignored.

## The technical decisions

**Rust from end to end, from the server to the three client targets.** The backend is written in Axum with PostgreSQL; the client, in Dioxus, compiles to WebAssembly for the web and to native binaries for desktop and mobile. The domain and application layers form a single body of code shared between the server and the three client targets: a business rule exists once, not once per platform. That is what lets me carry the three targets in parallel without tripling the work, a point that matters when you are alone on the project.

**The hexagonal dependency rule is enforced by a blocking CI gate, not just by the folder structure.** The pure domain is split into crates by layer, and beyond what the compiler already enforces, a blocking CI gate analyses the `cargo metadata` graph and runs dedicated clippy lints to reject any dependency that would break the direction of the arrows. On a long-running project that I carry alone, I prefer an automatic wall to a discipline I would have to keep reminding myself of.

**The product is split into fault-isolated cells rather than into horizontal layers.** Cœur Suite, AI, Plugin-host and Mail are four independent macro-units, each testable on its own, and none reads another's database: each cell defines its own degraded mode. The promise "if the AI goes down, the calendar keeps working" is a consequence of this topology, not an intention that would have to be checked by hand at every change.

**Synchronisation shows conflicts rather than silently overwriting them.** A generic synchronisation core, based on ETags and on external identifiers carried by sync links, resolves conflicts using last-write-wins but makes them visible rather than letting them disappear. This loop was first proven in its entirety on the narrowest possible case, two-way synchronisation with Google Calendar, delivered as MVP1 in June 2026, before being extended to the other sources.

**The infrastructure is self-hosted and containerised rather than delegated to a PaaS.** The repository runs on a GitLab instance of my own (git.kovelt.fr); production runs on Hetzner Cloud behind a Caddy reverse proxy that handles TLS automatically, in Docker/Podman containers; CI/CD runs for now on the development machine, with a layer cache through cargo-chef, until a dedicated build VPS is available for the beta. It is the same logic as the one applied to the user's data: control the hosting chain from end to end rather than entrust it entirely to a third party.

**Every structural decision is recorded in a journal that is never rewritten.** More than forty-eight ADRs document the decisions with their context and alternatives, and a correction is always added as a new dated entry rather than replacing the old one. Above this journal, a Constitution fixes the product's identity and a handful of non-negotiable refusals, including never imposing Google as a login identifier. The renaming of Chronos to Vefta, in July 2026, went through the same channel: a full prior-art search revealed a near-homophony with Kronos, a player in workforce management, and a name that had become too narrow for a suite that goes well beyond the calendar. The corresponding ADR documents the decision rather than simply renaming a repository.

## What I learned from it

That the discipline that lasts is the one the tooling enforces, not the one you promise yourself: the CI gate on the architecture and the immutable ADR journal play, when working solo, the role that peer review would play in a team. That a thin end-to-end slice, proving the whole chain on the simplest case before widening it, costs less to correct than a system built in breadth before being proven in depth: that is why Google synchronisation was proven only on the calendar before being extended elsewhere. And that deliberately freezing the construction of an already designed workstream behind a measurable trigger, as with the professional Teams back office, avoids design debt without giving up on having thought it through.

## In figures

- More than 48 immutable ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
- 4 independent macro cells: Cœur Suite, AI, Plugin-host, Mail
- MVP1 delivered in June 2026: native foundation + two-way Google synchronisation
- Renaming of Chronos to Vefta decided in July 2026, with a full prior-art search
- 2 ROCm toolchains compared for fine-tuning the on-device SLM (Mistral 7B, QLoRA)

UHA Learn is my storyline project (fil rouge) for the first year of the UHA 4.0.1 programme, before MomoCad, my storyline project for the second year. The brief asks for a complete website, built alone, around third-party data, from HTML and CSS up to an in-house PHP API, with Git, a MySQL database and a deployment script.

The project was delivered and defended in December 2025. It has not been maintained since: it is a closed chapter, and my first project carried out alone from start to finish.

## The problem

The 4.0.1 storyline exercise is designed as a progression: start from an HTML and CSS mock-up, read a third-party API's data and then display it dynamically, build a relational database and my own PHP API, with CRUD, security and documentation at every stage.

Rather than pick a theme unrelated to my everyday life, I built a tool for my own course. UHA 4.0 publishes an institutional API, `filrouge.uha4point0.fr`, which lists the years of the programme (from 4.0.0 to 4.0.3) and their courses. I built UHA Learn around that source: a course catalogue that can be browsed by year, personal progress tracking, a moderated queue of course proposals, and an administration panel.

The real problem was keeping this whole stack going alone without cutting corners, particularly on the backend: writing the REST API in PHP without a framework to understand what a framework usually does on my behalf, and delivering a deployment script that genuinely works somewhere other than on my machine, not only in front of the jury.

## The technical decisions

**The REST backend is written in PHP without a framework, with an MVC architecture set up by hand.** Controllers, Models, Middleware (CORS, JWT authentication), Routes and Utils make up the five folders of the backend, for nineteen PHP files and about four thousand four hundred lines. The aim was not to avoid a framework on principle, but to understand the routing, the normalised response format and the database access that a framework usually hides, before I could judge what it would really bring me.

**Authentication combines JWT access and refresh tokens, three roles and account statuses.** Student, moderator and administrator do not have the same rights, and an account can be active, suspended or graduated. Each of the roughly thirty-five endpoints of the API is documented in the README with its required access level, public, authenticated, moderator or administrator: a list of endpoints without that column says nothing about real security.

**The seed scripts are an operations tool, not a throwaway script.** `seed_all.php` accepts `--api-only` to import the real years and courses from the institutional API, `--test-only` to generate a set of test accounts (seven students with various statuses, three moderators, one administrator), and `--clean` to remove everything. The admin panel exposes the same logic behind a secured API: database status, running the scripts, cleaning, resetting. A database that can only be rebuilt by hand is a database you end up afraid to touch.

**The deployment script adapts to the Linux distribution rather than imposing mine.** `deploy.sh` detects the package manager (apt, dnf, yum, pacman, zypper), configures SELinux on Fedora and RHEL, avoids port conflicts, migrates and seeds the database, with `--auto`, `--update` and `--uninstall` modes. A one-command `install.sh` detects and installs Docker and Git, then clones and deploys the project. Going beyond the brief's plain requirement of a Bash script had a precise purpose: that a classmate on another distribution gets the same result without reading a line of the script.

**The catalogue is designed to be searched, not merely listed.** The advanced search covers title, category, year and required tools, and the catalogue is paginated. With four years of training and several courses per year, a single list with no filter or pagination would have become unreadable by the second year of content.

## What I learned from it

Writing the MVC by hand taught me what a PHP framework actually does: route a request, standardise a response, protect access through middleware. I have kept that yardstick whenever I have evaluated a framework since, to know what it really spares me rather than what it hides from me.

It is also my first project carried out alone from start to finish, from the first line of code to the deployment script, before the teamwork on code inherited from HEHEWATT and the client relationship of AUTOFIN Control. No box in the brief required me to industrialise and document: I did it because a project that can only be installed by explaining every step aloud is not really finished, and because an authentication guide written with analogies for a beginner reader was meant to be useful to the other students of the cohort, not only to me.

Trace 4.0 is the official Chrome extension of UHA 4.0 that measures the time logged-in students are actually active on the training resources. It was built on Manifest V2, the format Chrome ended up switching off. In early 2026, on my own initiative and outside any graded coursework, I migrated the extension to Manifest V3 single-handedly, delivered in a single iteration (v1.2.0) with a changelog that documents every file changed.

## The problem

For each logged-in student, the extension tracks the time spent on the resources listed by the training platform: UHA credentials, a terms-of-use (CGU) checkbox, a visible toggle button, and an icon that changes colour with the state (green active, red inactive, grey logged out). The measured sessions are sent back to an internal API of the school, and the student finds their programmes, their courses and their history from the popup.

The problem was not functional but one of infrastructure: Manifest V2, the format it was built on, has been progressively switched off by Google in up-to-date browsers. Without intervention, the tracking tool refused to load, and nobody on the course could use it any more.

I took the initiative to migrate the extension in my own time. The difficulty is not renaming a few keys in the manifest: Manifest V3 changes the execution model. The background script is no longer a persistent page whose state stays readable at any moment, but an ephemeral service worker that Chrome kills and restarts as it sees fit. Everything that assumed an in-memory state available at all times had to be rethought.

## The technical decisions

**The service worker no longer has a reliable state, so all storage becomes asynchronous.** `localStorage`, being synchronous, is not accessible to a service worker. I replaced it everywhere with the asynchronous `chrome.storage.local`, behind two small wrappers, `getStorageData`/`setStorageData`, built on `Promise`s. The change cascades: the three files that read the state (`background.js`, `manager.js`, `gandalf.js`) are converted entirely to `async`/`await`, without changing the observable behaviour.

**Periodic tasks do not live in the service worker.** The classic trap of an MV3 migration is to put a `setInterval` in the background script: Chrome shuts down an idle service worker after about thirty seconds, which would interrupt it. `background.js` contains none. The polling for URL changes (`setInterval(checkUrlChange, 100)`) and the batched sending every two minutes (`sendPeriod = 2 * 60 * 1000`) live entirely in the content script `activityWatcher.js`, an ordinary page context that this shutdown does not affect. There is no need for `chrome.alarms`: the right execution context is enough.

**Changing the icon from a service worker means redrawing the image by hand.** `setIcon` can no longer take a direct file path. The `updateIcon` function in `background.js` fetches the PNG with `fetch`, converts it to an `ImageBitmap`, draws it onto a 128-pixel `OffscreenCanvas`, extracts the `ImageData` from it, and that result is what `chrome.action.setIcon` accepts. A constraint that looks minor on paper becomes the trickiest detail of the migration.

**The API configuration comes from the manifest, not from a copied constant.** Rather than hard-coding the address of the API, the code reads it back dynamically with `chrome.runtime.getManifest().host_permissions[0]`. The single source remains the manifest. The calculation is, however, copied identically into the three files that need it rather than factored into a shared module, a debt I describe below.

**Two communication channels coexist rather than one.** Continuous tracking goes through a named `Port`, `"Tracing"`, opened once by `activityWatcher.js` and kept for the life of the page, so that the service worker receives the `ACTIVITY`/`URL_CHANGE` events at no extra cost. One-off events (after a login, a logout, a change of the tracking button, or a click on "Mes formations") go through a second channel, `chrome.runtime.sendMessage({type: 'REFRESH_TRACKING'})`, called from three files (`gandalf.js`, `manager.js` and `P_index.js`) and received by a dedicated `chrome.runtime.onMessage` in `background.js`. I did not merge the two because they do not have the same lifespan: the first lasts the browsing session on a page, the second is a one-way message triggered by a user action.

## What I learned from it

That the Chrome extension platform has a precise security and execution model, and that knowing it in detail (the split between `permissions` and `host_permissions`, the object format of the CSP, the service worker lifecycle) changes the way you read any extension, not just this one. That taking over existing code without changing its behaviour is a different exercise from writing from scratch: you first have to understand what is there before deciding what must change. And that constraints that seem trivial on paper, such as changing an icon, are sometimes the ones that demand the most technical workarounds.

What I would do differently: the storage wrappers and the reading of the URL from the manifest are duplicated identically in three files, for lack of a common storage module. On a project of this size nothing broke, but it is exactly the kind of duplication I would factor out from the start today.

- vendored third-party libraries (jQuery slim, Bootstrap 4, Popper, Moment.js, Font Awesome kit): ≈14,931 lines, of which 14,876 for Moment.js alone

MomoCad is my storyline project (fil rouge) for the second year of the UHA 4.0.2 programme. The brief asks for an application and an API that manage geometric shapes in object-oriented programming: creating and deleting shapes, composing groups of them, computing their mathematical properties, and letting a language model query the data. The name comes from "Morgan" and AutoCAD, the tool that inspired the angle I chose.

As of 26 October 2026, the first delivery, the domain core, is written and fully covered by tests. The following deliveries, the API and its database, the workstation, the synchronisation and the chatbot, are specified and waiting their turn.

## The problem

The brief is designed for a drawing application or a tangram-style game served by a website. I wanted to make something else of it: a small 2D drawing program that behaves like a CAD tool. Shapes are assembled by union and subtraction, and the composite shape that results remembers the shapes it comes from. That is what makes the project interesting to build, because a composition is no longer a simple list of objects but a history of operations.

Two departures from the brief were discussed and approved with my supervisor: a desktop application rather than a website, and local operation first, with synchronisation to a server. The hosted API and database are still owed, as in the brief, and so is the chatbot.

The real technical problem is then this: how do you represent a drawing so that undo, history and synchronisation between several workstations are not features bolted on afterwards, but natural consequences of the model?

## The technical decisions

**Nothing is stored as state, everything is journal.** Every action of the person drawing becomes an event appended to a journal that only grows. The displayed state is a replay of that journal from the beginning. The method that applies an event is the same whether one acts or replays: there can therefore be no gap between what you see after drawing and what you get by rebuilding the drawing from scratch. A test replays the same journal twice and compares the results. History, undo and synchronisation become reads of the journal, not separate mechanisms.

**The hexagonal architecture is guaranteed by the compiler, not by a convention.** The domain core project references no external package, and the methods that modify a shape or a drawing are internal to the project: only the command handlers and the replay can call them, and the tests reach them through an explicit visibility grant. A host, whether console, API or graphical interface, physically cannot modify a drawing by bypassing a command. The dependency graph between the ten projects of the solution was laid down on the first day, before the adapters existed.

**Invariants are written in positive logic.** To reject an invalid radius, the code tests "is not strictly positive" rather than "is less than or equal to zero". The difference matters for a value that is not a number: every comparison with it is false, and the negative form would have let the radius through. The tests check the edge cases with non-numeric and infinite values.

**The geometry is computed by the domain, not delegated.** The area of a polygon comes from the shoelace formula, a circle is discretised into one hundred and twenty-eight segments with a measured relative error, and the coordinates are recentred before computation to keep floating-point precision far from the origin. The Clipper2 library will only be used for the union and subtraction of outlines, behind a port of the domain. While preparing this adapter, I found that the library's official documentation gave a wrong argument order for one of its functions, checked directly against the binary, and I recorded it before writing a single line.

**The tests are reviewed through mutation.** Deliberately breaking the code and watching whether a test fails led me to bracket each tolerance with two tests, one that rejects a value a thousand times smaller and one that accepts the limit value, and to check the content of error messages rather than just their type. The 100% coverage is measured by tooling, not asserted in a README.

**Documentation comes before code.** Nine PlantUML diagrams were written before the classes, then split into four views because a single sheet was no longer readable. The project's vocabulary is fixed in a ubiquitous language, and the documentation itself went through a cross-audit: one hundred and fifty-one raw findings, seventy-seven confirmed by independent verifiers, eighteen scoping decisions settled.

## What I learned from it

That a model chosen for a simple reason, keeping a record of a drawing's operations, gives me for free features I would otherwise have cobbled together one by one. That the strongest safeguards are the ones the compiler imposes, not the ones we promise ourselves to respect. That testing also means trying to make your own tests lie. And that a solo project copes very well with team discipline, independent reviews included, provided you formalise it.

What I would do differently: merge the working branch into the main branch earlier and commit the documentation as I go, rather than leaving one hundred and ninety-five pages outside the repository.

| 0. Specify the MVP in UML | Backlog, wireframe, pseudo-code for the area of a composite shape, validated user story |
| 1. Classes | `Rectangle`, `Triangle`, `Cercle`, instantiated in the console host |
| 2. Encapsulation | Public accessors, internal modifiers callable only by a command or the replay |
| 3. Inheritance | Abstract `Forme`, polymorphism demonstrated by a single loop and tested |
| 4. UML | Nine PlantUML diagrams, four class views |

HEHEWATT is a carpooling application developed as part of the E-mersion project, which brings together the Lycée Jean-Jacques Henner in Altkirch and UHA 4.0, funded by Noria. The repository has existed since October 2024 and has been taken over by several successive cohorts: more than a thousand commits, between thirty and fifty contributors. I joined in early 2026 as a full-stack developer on the domain core of the trips and on the notification system, with about 93 commits, as one of the first four contributors.

My work on HEHEWATT ends with my first year; the project continues to be taken over by the following cohorts, which has weighed on some of my decisions, documentation above all, since it is written for someone I will never meet.

## The problem

The Lycée Jean-Jacques Henner is located in the Sundgau, a rural area of the Haut-Rhin badly served by public transport: staff, parents and pupils make the same home-to-school journey by car every day, often alone. HEHEWATT connects these users: drivers publish one-off or recurring trips with intermediate stops, passengers book a seat on the trip that passes near their home, and an administrator on the school's side validates the accounts. The school is a partner of the project, not a client: no invoicing, just a real need to serve for its community.

The technical problem I ran into is not that of a project starting from scratch, but that of a PHP repository without a major framework, where each file is a page or an API endpoint, written by hand by dozens of people of very different levels over more than a year. The task was to add structural features, namely multiple stops with booking by segment and recurring trips compatible with the school calendar, without breaking what real users already rely on. The E-mersion programme aims for secondary-school pupils eventually to contribute to the code from their browser (a web IDE service exists in the Docker environment, commented out for now): documenting and splitting up the work is not an optional nicety.

## The technical decisions

**A booking uses up one seat per segment of the trip, not on the whole trip.** A trip with multiple stops loses its purpose if a passenger who gets on at the second stop and off at the third blocks a seat for the entire trip. The model therefore attaches to each booking a boarding stop and an alighting stop, and availability is computed segment by segment (`Stop::getAvailableSeats()`) rather than globally. I added the display of this per-segment occupancy to the trip card component shared by the five screens concerned, so that a driver can see at a glance which segment is full.

**Trip recurrence follows the real school calendar, not a bare weekly rule.** "Every Monday and Wednesday" means nothing during the holidays. The schema separates a recurring trip (`trajet_recurrent`) from its exceptions (`trip_exceptions`), with the same logic on the booking side (`reservation_recurrente` / `reservation_exceptions`), and cross-references all of this with two school calendar tables, `planning_annee_scolaire` and `planning_conges`, rather than hard-coding the holidays. On the booking side, I lifted a uniqueness constraint so that a passenger can sign up for the whole year or for single occasions on the same recurring trip, and wrote the day-list queries that follow from it.

**Most transactional emails go through a single service that covers the whole life cycle of a trip.** Of about fifteen files able to trigger an email, `NotificationService` (`api/services/`) centralises about twenty methods and queries the database with PDO prepared statements, not concatenated strings. Two rough edges remain unresolved: password reset calls `EmailService` directly, without going through it, and a second, unrelated `NotificationService` class (in-app notifications, `api/notification/`, unsigned) carries the same name in the same global namespace. This is the code I am most certain is mine: the headers of `NotificationService.php` and of the email configuration carry my name, unlike most of the rest of the repository, which is not attributed by name.

**Geolocation relies solely on free OpenStreetMap services, with no commercial API.** There was no budget for a paid key: Nominatim geocodes addresses within an area restricted to the Haut-Rhin and the neighbouring départements (Bas-Rhin, Vosges, Territoire de Belfort, Switzerland, Germany), OSRM computes travel times between stops, and Leaflet displays everything on a map. The real work was composing two APIs with different constraints: Nominatim limits requests to one per second (debounce, cache in `autocomplete.js`), and OSRM expects its coordinates as `longitude,latitude`, the reverse order, an inversion documented in `route-calculator.js` after I found it while spending hours debugging wrong arrival times.

**A versioned v1 API is added alongside the existing endpoints rather than replacing them.** In a repository where dozens of people already call the old endpoints, rewriting them all at once would have broken everyone's work. I created the CRUD endpoints of this v1 API, grouped by resource: trips (4), bookings (6), stops (5). They can respond with plain JSON or with pre-rendered HTML fragments for the pages already using AJAX, without touching the existing endpoints. The two APIs still coexist today.

## What I learned from it

This project taught me above all what "working in a team" means when the team changes its make-up every few weeks. A well-made feature delivered in one block helps nobody else if nobody can build on it: I learned to split my work into pieces small enough for a contributor who does not know the project's history to pick one up without rereading everything.

I also had to correct a reflex: when part of the team was not very active, I tended to fill the gap with personal work, with massive help from AI tools, rather than adapting the scope or reopening the allocation of tasks. The result: too many simultaneous changes make the work hard to follow, and a person who absorbs everything bears the responsibility alone, which is healthy for no one.

The most concrete lesson concerns structural changes: modifying a configuration file shared by the whole team's environment and by the school's servers, without flagging it or having it validated, can break the work of dozens of people who never asked for it. I now communicate this kind of change before merging it, not just in the commit message.

What I would do differently: systematically prepare the progress reviews, even for audiences less visible than a client, namely the pupils who will take over the project, and aim for smaller, more regular deliveries rather than impressive but disruptive leaps forward for the team.

- 1,058 commits across the whole repository, about 93 of them mine, as one of the first four contributors
- Between 30 and 50 contributors depending on the cohort, over 16 months (October 2024 to February 2026)
- 262 files excluding dependencies: about 26,000 lines of PHP (144 files), 13,500 lines of JS, 4,700 lines of CSS, 1,000 lines of Twig

GeoForge is a geometric puzzle web game; not to be confused with "GeoForge, the Godot addon", a terrain generation module that I developed separately and that shares only its name with this project. This one was my storyline project (fil rouge) for the second year of the UHA 4.0.2 programme, in the 2025-2026 academic year, carried out alone from February to April 2026 and defended before the jury. I have re-enrolled in 4.0.2 for 2026-2027, this time with MomoCad as the official storyline project.

## The problem

The 4.0.2 brief asks for an object-oriented application that manages geometric shapes: creating them, composing them, computing their characteristics. One of the suggested paths is a tangram-style game served by a website; I took that path literally and built an arcade puzzle against the clock, in which a target model made of several shapes must be rebuilt on a grid, within a time limit, with a fidelity score.

Because the game is competitive, with a leaderboard, a time limit and stars, the technical problem goes beyond the geometry itself. If the client alone decides that a placement is valid, or computes the score it sends to the server itself, nothing stops a player from tampering with their request to obtain an impossible score. A rule therefore had to be held strictly: the client previews and guides, but only the API decides, and it decides from a state it controls entirely, never from what the client claims to have achieved.

On top of this core, the project also had to work as a small platform: the levels are not only the ones I wrote, players can create their own, and someone has to review them before they are published. This second problem, editorial rather than algorithmic, called for a clear validation workflow rather than a "publish" button with no filter.

## The technical decisions

**The client decides neither whether a placement is valid nor the score: both are computed on the server, by a reproducible method.** In a timed, ranked game, letting the client judge validity or compute the score amounts to letting players mark their own work, and I wanted a reproducible, explainable result rather than an ad hoc grade. `IsPlacementValid` computes the grid cells occupied by a shape from a local mask rotated according to its rotation, and checks for placements outside the grid and for collisions; `AddShape()` and `MoveShape()` automatically roll back any operation that fails this check. The score comes from a fidelity percentage computed by a cell-by-cell comparison between the player's construction and the target model (occupied in both, by the right type of shape, in the right place), rather than from a formula worked out by hand; combined with a time bonus, this percentage feeds the score and its conversion into stars, from one to five. The client only displays a green or red preview, a prediction, never a decision.

**The domain knows neither the database nor HTTP.** I wanted to be able to test all the game logic without starting a server or a database, and to guarantee that a controller cannot contain a business rule that only it would know. `GeoForge.Core`, meaning the `Shape2D` shapes, seven concrete shapes and the `Shape2DFactory` factory, depends on no other project in the solution; `GeoForge.Api` (controllers, DTOs) and `GeoForge.Infrastructure` (EF Core, migrations) depend on it, never the reverse. The 131 xUnit unit tests run on this project alone, with no database or server to start.

**Player-created content follows a multi-state workflow, not a "publish" button.** A badly designed level, too easy, too hard, unplayable, degrades the experience of every other player; publishing without a filter was not acceptable. A level goes through draft, testing by its author, submission, moderation, accepted or refused, with an assigned difficulty, and then publication, all driven from an admin panel that also manages accounts and system levels.

**A level can be generated by an algorithm, and its difficulty assessed automatically, without going through a human each time.** Hand-writing every level of a growing catalogue does not scale, and judging difficulty "by eye" does not give a consistent ranking from one level to the next. Alongside the moderation workflow above, the admin panel exposes a procedural level generator and an automatic assessment of their difficulty, two algorithms that go beyond the scope of a classic CRUD.

**Authentication has to withstand more than a forgotten password.** A system of accounts and a leaderboard is a natural target for automated login attempts if nothing slows them down. It relies on JWT tokens, passwords hashed with BCrypt and roles that protect the sensitive routes; after three failed logins, an account is locked for fifteen minutes before another attempt is allowed.

**Phaser stayed an engine walled off in its own corner, not mixed in with the rest of React.** A Phaser canvas mounted and unmounted in step with React's lifecycle, through re-renders and navigation between pages, easily creates ghost instances of the game that keep running in the background. The game's scenes (`GameScene`, `ShapeRenderer`) live behind a stable boundary, and the state of the current game is mirrored in the Zustand store `gameStore`: the rest of the interface, meaning the displayed timer, the buttons and the modals, never needs to read the inside of the canvas to know where the game stands.

## What I learned from it

That the rule "the client decides nothing" is simpler to put in place from the first controller than to add after the fact: because placement validation and scoring were on the server from the start, I never had to go back to close a cheating loophole. That integrating a game engine into a web application is not a mere wiring detail: Phaser and React each have their own idea of who owns the display, and the only way to avoid conflicts is to decide explicitly, once, where the boundary runs, rather than redraw it at every bug. That documenting an algorithm before the defence forces you to check that you truly understand it yourself, not just that it compiles and passes the tests. And that setting myself a written framework for the use of AI, with the explicit goal of being able to re-explain and redo everything without help, changed the way I work more than any architectural choice.

GeoForge is an open source addon that I am developing for Godot 4, which generates terrain from real geographic data or from manual sculpting in the editor. I should clarify the name straight away: another of my projects, my second-year storyline project (fil rouge), is also called GeoForge (a geometric puzzle in React and Phaser). The two share only the name; the one discussed here is the Godot addon, in C#/.NET, a personal project under the MIT licence.

As of 26 October 2026, the project is in pre-alpha: around fifteen modules are defined, the rework of the water system is under way, and the GitHub repository exists but is still empty.

## The problem

Building a credible open world in a game engine normally takes dozens of hours of manual work: modelling the relief, tracing every river, drawing every road, planting every forest. Unity has mature terrain tools (Gaia Pro, R.A.M), Unreal a native water system. Godot, a fast-growing open source engine, has no complete equivalent, particularly on the .NET/C# side.

GeoForge tackles this gap through two entry points that must converge on the same representation of the terrain: a pipeline that downloads the geographic data of a real region (OpenStreetMap for roads, watercourses, forests and buildings, an SRTM elevation model for the relief) and turns it into playable terrain, and a suite of editing tools built into the Godot editor: sculpting the relief, tracing rivers and roads, painting biomes. It has to be possible to generate a region from OSM and then refine it by hand, or the other way round, without either path being a second-class citizen.

The real problem behind these two entry points is that of setting the parameters. A tool that asks the user to set the width of a river or the slope of an embankment by hand produces a laborious and rarely credible result, because real terrain obeys laws the user does not necessarily know. How can you get a credible result by default without depriving the user of control when they need it?

## The technical decisions

**Every parameter comes from a physical law or an engineering standard, never from an arbitrary choice.** The width and depth of a watercourse follow the hydraulic geometry of Leopold and Maddock, its velocity the Manning-Strickler formula, its sinuosity the Schumm classification; slopes respect the angle of repose of the materials, road design relies on soil bearing capacity (CBR) and on the reference documents of Cerema, SETRA and IDRRIM, and the condition of a road surface on the ASTM D-6433 standard. These values are never set by hand: they are derived. The flip side: every control point exposes nullable fields, so that the user takes the controls back exactly where they want to, and nowhere else.

**The generators do not know one another: they communicate only through the data they share.** Around fifteen modules (GeoCore for the foundations, then GeoMountain, GeoWater, GeoWay, GeoForest, GeoCity, GeoOSM...) read and write a heightmap and metadata layers managed by GeoCore, without ever referencing each other directly. Generation runs as a pipeline ordered by priority: the ground, the mountains, the craters, the water, the roads, the vegetation, the cities. A contributor adds a generator without touching the existing code, following the open/closed principle. That principle is embodied in six named design patterns: Strategy for the data source (`ITerrainDataProvider`), Factory for registering the generators, Observer for chunk loading, Command for undo/redo, Pipeline for ordering, Composite for GeoWater and GeoWay.

**All the interactive editors share the same skeleton.** Whether it sculpts the relief or traces a road, an editor rests on the same framework: a type enum and its static configuration, control points with nullable overrides, computed segment analyses, Godot Resources for the definition and the network, a controller with a state machine, a build service as a pipeline, a UI panel that communicates through signals. Understanding one editor means understanding all the others: the cognitive load does not grow with the number of editing tools.

**Diagnose before rewriting: the case of the river editor.** The first version traced a river as a spline: the user drew the path and set the altitude of each point by hand. The flaw lay upstream of the code: a drawing tool applied to a physical phenomenon, whereas water is not drawn, it flows. The rework adopts a flow-source paradigm: the user places a source, the system traces the gradient descent over the relief, carves the heightmap and builds the water mesh from the result. Before rewriting, I checked what already existed: the inherited `RiverGenerator` component already contained the right gradient-descent algorithm, so the rework keeps it and replaces only the editing front end. The rework document runs to about five hundred and fifty lines: breakdown into components, pseudocode, edge cases, phasing in three stages.

**Zero warnings tolerated, documentation mandatory by construction.** The project compiles with `TreatWarningsAsErrors`: a single warning breaks the build, which in effect makes XML documentation of every public API mandatory, since an undocumented method generates one. One class per file, a shared `.editorconfig`. Continuous integration (GitHub Actions) covers multi-OS builds, tests with coverage, C# formatting, Markdown lint, a security audit of the dependencies and a release pipeline. The same discipline applies to Git: branches `main` → `develop` → feature, commits in Conventional Commits format (for example `feat(river): add flow simulation`), pull requests and squash merges every time, semantic versioning. A personal project has no assigned reviewer; it is the tooling that plays that role.

**Design comes before code.** More than twenty architecture documents were written before the first class, each following the same template: overview, user workflow, physical basis, C# data model, interface mock-up, V1/V2/V3 phasing, known limits. This template makes decisions traceable, records the build-up of my skills and turns implementation into guided execution rather than improvisation.

## What I learned from it

The river editor work taught me two lessons that I reuse elsewhere in the project. First, a tool's mental model must match the physics of the phenomenon it manipulates: a drawing tool applied to a flow produces friction and a barely credible result, however good the interface. DevEye is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server written in Rust that gives an AI agent (Claude Code in particular, though any MCP client will do) the ability to observe and drive a live graphical application: screenshots, clicks, typing, state inspection, log reading, conditional waits. The agent uses it like any other tool, with no human intervention.

The project is private (a personal GitLab repository, Kovelt Utilities) and has been under development since June 2026. Milestones M0 to M7 have been delivered since the end of June, and development continues in sprints that extend the tools. An open-source release is planned for version 1.0, once the tool is stable.

## The problem

An AI agent that can read and write code has neither eyes nor hands in front of a graphical application: it cannot see what its last change produced on screen, cannot click a button, cannot tell that a UI is broken. For the web, bridges already exist (Playwright and automated browsers). For native desktop applications, particularly in the Rust/Dioxus ecosystem that I use for my own products, nothing comparable existed.

I built DevEye to fill that gap, as a cross-cutting tool rather than a throwaway script for a single project: it already serves as tooling for my other products, and its target is not a single UI technology but every one I use or might use.

The technical problem that follows is to bring together, under a single abstraction, ways of driving an interface that have almost nothing in common: the DevTools protocol of a Chromium browser, a custom-built HTTP bridge embedded in the target app, the D-Bus screen capture of a Wayland compositor and, when there is neither a browser nor an embedded SDK, input injection at the level of the system itself, on Wayland, an ecosystem designed precisely to prevent that kind of injection.

## The technical decisions

**The core knows no driving technology, only ports.** `deveye-core` is a pure domain (`Snapshot`, `InteractionCommand`, `LogEvent`) without a single technical dependency, and `deveye-ports` defines twelve Rust traits (`Renderer`, `AppInspector`, `InteractionSink`, `JsEvaluator`, `LogSource`, `CommandRouter`, `WaitCondition`, `WindowManager`, `Clipboard`…) that ten adapters each implement for a different technology. Adding a new target means writing one more adapter, never touching the core or the forty-one MCP tools built on the ports: hexagonal architecture, tested on a real case and not merely stated as a principle.

**Four targeting modes choose the technology, never the agent.** The `cdp` mode talks to the Chrome DevTools Protocol for any Chromium WebView, `sdk` goes through a custom-built HTTP bridge that an app embeds in one line, `kwin-eis` injects input at the system level for apps with neither a WebView nor an SDK (the "eyes" then go through screen capture), and `auto` tries `cdp` first and switches call by call to `sdk` as soon as the first one fails. I did not want the agent driving DevEye to have to know which technology is answering on the other side.

**Input injection on Wayland goes through the official KWin EIS portal, in pure Rust, without FFI.** Wayland is designed to prevent one application from injecting input into another: no XWayland to get around, no `uinput` to open directly. The only legitimate path is the `org.kde.KWin.EIS.RemoteDesktop` portal, implemented with the `reis` crate. It is negotiated over a D-Bus connection that must stay open, or the handshake simply ends in an EOF, a protocol pitfall that I discovered by running into it. On the keyboard side, each Unicode keysym must be resolved to an evdev keycode through `xkbcommon` before it can be injected. This is the most intricate part of the project.

**The "dev tool" posture is defended in depth, not merely declared in a README.** `deveye_sdk::init()` compiles no DevEye code outside `debug_assertions`, even if the integrator forgets their `#[cfg]`; the server binds only to loopback (`127.0.0.1`, never `0.0.0.0`) and rejects any non-local `Host` header with a 403, before any route; CORS is deny-all and the exposed crates carry `#[forbid(unsafe_code)]`. The JS evaluation queue is bounded and answers 503 rather than letting memory grow if the target app is frozen, and the log buffer is capped by overwriting the oldest entries. Each mechanism addresses one specific way of leaking into production, not a generic risk.

**The tool is audited with the rigour it applies to other people's code.** A formal internal audit that I carried out after milestone M7 produced one hundred and eight prioritised findings, including blocking gates, followed by a second audit in July. The CI, on my own self-hosted GitLab runner, runs `cargo fmt --check`, `clippy` with `-D warnings` and the workspace tests, plus `cargo-deny` to audit dependencies and licences; the tests that need a real Wayland session are isolated with `#[ignore]`.

## What I learned from it

That fitting four driving technologies under a single abstraction forces you to name precisely what they have in common, a render, an input, a wait, rather than stacking them behind special cases. That wait primitives are the real key to the reliability of an agent loop: an AI agent chains actions far faster than a human, so I had to serialise the MCP calls and wait for an explicit condition rather than a fixed delay for the loop to hold up. And that designing for an agent as the end user is a discipline of its own: the forty-one tools have precise contracts and structured returns that I designed to be understood and chained by an LLM, not read by a human, a form of UX whose user is not human.

- 41 MCP tools in six families, on 12 ports and 10 adapters
- 4 driving channels: CDP, embedded SDK bridge, KWin capture, KWin EIS injection
- 65 commits between June and July 2026, milestones M0 to M7 delivered on 25 June (a figure for that phase; development has continued since in sprints that extend the tools)

chronos-penpot-tools is a plugin for Penpot, the open source alternative to Figma, that generates a Dioxus (RSX) component in Rust from a mock-up selected in the editor. I built it to provide tooling for my own product: when I wrote v0.1, that product was still called Chronos; it became Vefta in July 2026. The plugin itself keeps its original name for now; renaming it has not been done yet.

The project is private and remains a prototype. v0.1, delivered in February 2026, covers shapes, text and flexible layouts; a versioned roadmap runs up to a v0.5. The MIT licence is in place from the start, but publication as open source for the Rust and Dioxus community is planned only for v1.0.

## The problem

Dioxus is a cross-platform Rust framework for user interfaces — desktop, web, mobile — whose rendering syntax is called RSX. Penpot is an interface design tool, the open equivalent of Figma. Between the two there is no bridge: going from a Penpot mock-up to a Dioxus component is done by hand, screen by screen, reading through every layer to work out the structure and the styles.

For Chronos, the cross-platform application in Rust and Dioxus that I am developing separately, this manual translation came up again with every new screen. I built the bridge myself: a Penpot plugin that reads the user's selection and generates the corresponding Dioxus RSX component, ready to paste into the code. A "Figma-to-code", but for an open source ecosystem and a target, Rust, that no tool of this kind covers.

The real problem is not reading a Penpot JSON file: it is getting from a tree of layers designed for a visual editor to code that a Rust developer will want to keep as it is, without locking the translation into a step that would rule out any future extension to other targets or other ways of styling.

## The technical decisions

**All the conversion logic lives in a Rust crate compiled to WebAssembly, never in the plugin's TypeScript.** The plugin runs in Penpot's sandboxed iframe, but the translation of a tree of layers into a Dioxus component is a separate crate, `penpot-to-dioxus`, called from the TypeScript through `wasm-bindgen`. There are two reasons for this split: the complex logic stays in a typed language, testable with `cargo test` independently of the browser, and the crate is designed to be reusable outside the plugin, as a CLI or directly in the tooling of Chronos/Vefta. The crate is built as both `cdylib`, for the WebAssembly, and `rlib`, for the tests, and is compiled with `opt-level = "s"`, LTO and strip to keep the WASM binary small.

**The converter goes through an intermediate representation rather than translating the Penpot JSON into RSX directly.** The crate is structured like a small compiler in six modules: `parser.rs` deserialises the Penpot JSON, through serde, into a typed `PenpotNode` tree — fills, strokes, effects, flex and grid layouts, text, component information; `transform.rs` converts that tree into the `DioxusNode` intermediate representation, with heuristics such as choosing between `h1` to `h4`, `p` or `span` according to the font size of a piece of text; `rsx_builder.rs` produces the final RSX code, indented and readable; `styles.rs` translates the visual properties into CSS — hexadecimal colours to rgba, gradients, alignments, grid tracks; `svg_extract.rs`, planned for v0.4, will detect the shapes to be exported as SVG; `lib.rs` is the crate's entry point, which exposes the function `#[wasm_bindgen] fn convert(json, options)` called from the TypeScript. Going through this intermediate representation rather than a direct translation makes the generator extensible to new targets and new styling modes, and makes it testable module by module.

**The TypeScript plugin is split into two worlds that communicate only by messages.** Penpot's Plugin API imposes this separation: `plugin.ts` is the only file with access to the `penpot` API, it reads the selection and serialises the design tree; `main.ts` is the iframe's user interface, which initialises the WebAssembly module and displays the preview of the generated code with copy and download; `wasm-bridge.ts` loads that module asynchronously. This boundary limits the surface that touches the user's actual document, and the plugin asks only for the minimal `content:read` permission: it is deliberately read-only, and cannot modify anything in the source design.

**The specification comes before the code: a mapping table and a negative scope were written before the first line of Rust.** `MAPPING.md` fixes the philosophy of the conversion — visual fidelity first, idiomatic code that can be edited by hand, no raw HTML dump, semantic naming derived from the layers — and a versioned roadmap runs from v0.1 (shapes, text, flex) to v0.5 (CSS classes and pattern detection), by way of Penpot components, typed props, grids, gradients and shadows, then SVG export. The negative scope is explicitly stated: no generation of business logic, no automatic responsive behaviour in v1. The known limitations are documented as localised TODOs in the code, by file and function, rather than hidden.

**The MIT licence is in place from v0.1, but publication as open source is deferred to v1.0.** The tool was born of an internal need, to provide tooling for Chronos/Vefta, and remains a private repository on my personal self-hosted GitLab until the generator has reached its full roadmap. The licence is chosen from the start so as not to have to come back to it later, but I would rather deliver a tool that keeps its promises to the Rust/Dioxus community than a half-finished plugin already carrying a public name.

## What I learned from it

That building the conversion crate as a pure Rust module, verifiable with `cargo test` without a browser or an iframe, avoids debugging the translation logic and the WebAssembly plumbing at the same time: when a test in `transform.rs` fails, I already know it is not a problem of WASM loading or `postMessage`. That the step easiest to skip out of impatience is also the most expensive to skip: `MAPPING.md` and its negative scope, written before the first line of Rust, set the requirement of idiomatic RSX and the explicit refusal of the raw HTML dump as a principle of the project from the start, not as a constraint to be rediscovered as the code goes along. That choosing an intermediate representation rather than a direct translation has an immediate cost, six modules instead of a single file that does everything, but that this cost disappears as soon as you want to add a target or a styling mode, which v0.4 and v0.5 will do without touching the core already written. And that building the tool my own product needs, rather than making do with existing tools, brought me into Rust and WebAssembly through the most demanding door: understanding a complete compilation chain, from `wasm-pack` to two separate Vite entry points, before it becomes invisible.

## In figures

- Rust crate `penpot-to-dioxus`: about 1,400 lines, 6 modules, compiled to WebAssembly
- TypeScript plugin: about 500 lines, built with Vite
- 4 design documents, including `MAPPING.md`
- v0.1 (MVP) delivered in February 2026; versioned roadmap up to v0.5
- MIT licence in place from v0.1

carbon-fr is an open source civic API that exposes the carbon intensity of French electricity in real time, nationally and for the twelve regions, with a public dashboard. It is the French equivalent of the British carbonintensity.org.uk, a service that did not exist in France even though the open data it needs — RTE, ADEME, ENTSO-E — is among the best in Europe. Dual MIT / Apache-2.0 licence, listed as a reuse on data.gouv.fr.

As of 26 October 2026, the project is at version 0.11.0, stable: 30 documented endpoints, a public dashboard, a published TypeScript SDK. I design, develop and host it on my own, and I keep developing it.

## The problem

For several years the United Kingdom has had carbonintensity.org.uk, a national carbon intensity API that has become the reference infrastructure for *carbon-aware computing*: shifting computation to the hours when electricity is least carbon-intensive. France had nothing comparable. RTE publishes excellent raw data, éCO2mix, through the ODRÉ platform — but no stable, documented, regionalised civic API made it usable by developers or integrators.

The use cases, meanwhile, kept multiplying without an answer. The responsible digital movement (Boavizta, GreenIT.fr) wants to schedule its computation in low-carbon slots. The hydrogen sector needs to know, hour by hour, whether grid electricity makes an electrolyser eligible under the RFNBO or low-carbon regulatory frameworks. More broadly, nobody could easily access the breakdown of the electricity price or properly sourced references for the cost of generation.

So the problem was not a lack of data but a lack of an instrument: data scattered across several producers, revised over time, methodologically ambiguous — direct emissions or life-cycle analysis? — and never served in a directly usable form. That is the gap carbon-fr fills, with one constraint set from the first commit: to remain a strictly neutral measuring instrument, one that exposes the data without ever settling the energy debates it informs.

## The technical decisions

**The architecture is hexagonal, to isolate the carbon calculation from sources that change without warning.** The domain (`core`, `eligibility`) is written in pure types with no external dependency; the adapters (ODRÉ, ENTSO-E, weather, forecast, GBDT, Postgres, axum, webhooks) plug into ports. Public data sources change format, frequency and availability without notice; the hexagonal architecture makes each source replaceable and testable in isolation. Evidence: a Cargo workspace of eleven crates and a single server binary.

**Every value carries a `vintage`, because RTE revises its own figures.** The same hour goes through three successive states — real-time, consolidated, final — with different values at each stage; a naive API would silently serve contradictory figures depending on when the request is made. Ingestion relies on an upsert with a composite key (region, timestamp, methodology), completed by a `vintage` field. A direct consequence: no ORM, persistence in native SQL through sqlx (queries checked at compile time), to keep fine control over these upserts.

**Regulatory thresholds are configuration data, never constants in the code.** The eligibility criteria (renewable share ≥ 90 % under Article 4, the surplus exception at €20/MWh, the low-carbon threshold at 64 g) come from European legal texts that evolve; they are versioned and parameterised rather than hard-coded, so that the API follows the texts without being rewritten.

**The legal granularity is not the physical granularity of the calculation.** Regulatory eligibility is assessed at the level of the national bidding zone, whereas carbon-fr calculates at regional level: the API therefore never presents a region as "eligible" as if that had a regulatory meaning of its own — it is only a finer display grid than the one that counts legally.

**No version of the forecasting model goes into production without passing a formal backtest gate.** RTE does not forecast the future: I model the forecast myself, with a climatological baseline model and a gradient boosting model (GBDT) fed by Open-Meteo weather data. This forecast feeds `/schedule` and the greenest window; changing it without control would mean basing scheduling decisions on a degraded model. Evidence: backtest gates set by ADR-0012 and ADR-0028.

**Neutrality is verified by an adversarial review; it is not simply declared.** I systematically serve the alternatives side by side rather than choose in the user's place: two carbon methodologies in parallel (`rte-direct`, `acv-ademe`), two hydrogen eligibility frameworks (RFNBO, low-carbon), LCOE as multi-source ranges. The most sensitive layers — the LCOE comparison (ADR-0024), the eligibility overlays (ADR-0026) — each have a dedicated, versioned neutrality review. The same standard applies to the code: v0.7.0 is an audit release that came out of a full adversarial review of the workspace, with nineteen confirmed defects fixed. And when the data is awkward — Brittany shows 329 g for generation when the national figure is 32 g — the answer is to document it, not to smooth it over: the region generates little, and what it generates is more carbon-intensive, which says nothing about what it consumes (ADR-0008); the consumption series `acv-ademe@2`, corrected for cross-border exchanges, completes the picture (ADR-0010).

## What I learned from it

I learned that neutrality is not a stance one puts on display but an engineering constraint one verifies: parameterising a threshold, providing two frameworks side by side, having a wording checked in an adversarial review are concrete acts, not declared intentions. I learned that documenting awkward data is better than smoothing it over: the Brittany case holds up because the explanation exists in writing before anyone needs it.

I also found that diligence about the licences of sources is an underrated skill in a solo open source project: checking what one is allowed to reuse, ruling out a source whose licence does not fit, auditing the dependencies on every CI run with `cargo-deny`. None of this is visible in the finished API, but it is one of the reasons the project can be cited as a reference on data.gouv.fr.

And that a solo project does not force you to give up team discipline: immutable ADRs and adversarial reviews play the role a peer review would have played. The v0.7.0 audit release, nineteen defects found and fixed, is the proof by result, not by intention alone.

- 30 endpoints under `/v1`, documented in OpenAPI
- Backend in Rust (2024 edition, tokio): Cargo workspace of eleven crates and one server binary, hexagonal architecture
- PostgreSQL persistence in native SQL (sqlx), no ORM
- Geographic coverage: national + 12 regions; 3 carbon methodologies served in parallel (`rte-direct`, `acv-ademe@1`, `acv-ademe@2`)

AUTOFIN Control is the client project of my first year on UHA 4.0: a desktop application for the financial control department of m2A, the Mulhouse conurbation. I built it with a team of five students between January and May 2026, and I was the lead developer: about 38% of the 393 commits, the architecture, the extraction pipeline, and a good share of the team's conventions and documentation.

The software was delivered to the client in three signed MSIX versions.

## The problem

Every year, the financial controllers at m2A check the accounts of the associations that the conurbation subsidises. Each association sends a balance sheet and an income statement as PDFs, produced by its own chartered accountant, so there are as many layouts as there are accounting firms. Until then, the work meant re-keying the amounts for the current and the previous financial year by hand into a standardised Excel tracking template: a long, repetitive task and, above all, a source of keying errors on figures where an error is not acceptable.

AUTOFIN Control automates this chain without taking the controller out of it: import the PDF, extract the accounting lines from it, have them checked and corrected visually, aggregate them, attach them to the right categories of the template, then export. One constraint was there from the start and weighed on every choice that followed: the associations' financial data must never leave the controller's workstation. No server, no cloud, no network call: a local SQLite database and processing on the machine, because this is public money and data belonging to third-party associations.

The real technical problem was not reading a PDF but reading it reliably despite layouts we do not control, with a team of five people of very different levels, for a client who was actually going to use it.

## The technical decisions

**The extraction reads the geometry of the PDF, not its raw text, and uses no AI at all.** Two other approaches existed before this one, a mode going through a local language model and a bridge to a Python script, and both were then removed from the project together, `LlmExtractionService` and `RegexGeneratorService` included, along with their NuGet dependencies. What remains is a five-phase pipeline that works only on the X/Y coordinates of the words: `WordRowGrouper` groups the words into rows, `RowCellParser` splits each row into cells, `ColumnPositionDetector` finds the numeric columns by clustering, `NetColumnIdentifier` tells the Net N and Net N-1 columns apart from the Gross and depreciation columns, and `AccountingLineExtractor` builds the final lines. The reason: in a financial control tool, the same PDF must always give the same result, and must stay explainable to someone who did not write the code, which a language model does not guarantee.

**The core of the domain depends on nothing, and you can check it by opening the project file.** `Autofin.Core` references no NuGet package, only models and service interfaces. `Autofin.Infrastructure` implements them (SQLite, ClosedXML, PDF extraction, mapping), and `Autofin.Client` assembles everything through a single dependency injection entry point. With five people of uneven levels in the same repository, this separation is what lets someone touch the extraction without risking breaking the export.

**An extracted line is attached to an accounting category by score, not by the first keyword found.** Labels change from one accounting firm to the next: different abbreviations, accents and capitalisation for the same concept. A simple "first keyword that matches" rule would have put too many lines in the wrong category. The engine normalises the label, adds up positive keywords, subtracts negative keywords that disqualify a category, and adds a bonus if an external configuration already recognises that label for that client. Sixty-three dedicated tests cover the eleven categories of the income statement and the twenty categories of the balance sheet. A second, more recent building block (tickets AC-343/AC-344), `ExcelCategoryReader` and `ExcelCategoryRepository`, reads the categories directly from the Excel workbook the controller imports, and is eventually meant to replace these hard-coded lists, which will survive only as a safety net.

**The Excel export pipeline was entirely redesigned along the way so that it never overwrites a formula in the client's workbook again.** The first version recreated part of the file at each export, at the risk of losing formulas already in place, including between sheets. Ticket AC-395 changed the contract: a new service, `ExcelInsertionExportService`, inserts only the columns for the current financial year, captures and then rewrites the existing formulas, and shifts the history to the right without touching it. The change is recorded in a dated decision log: 131 tests out of 131 pass after the switch.

**Technical debt was measured by audits commissioned from an AI tool, then verified and applied, not discovered by chance.** A global audit as early as February, revisited in March, then an audit per layer in April, with tickets ranked by impact and by effort. One of them put a number on a regression nobody had seen coming: a file of the aggregation page, supposed to stay around three hundred lines, had 922. The fix moved the business logic into the associated ViewModel and brought the file back down to 478 lines, nearly halved. It was moved more than eliminated: that ViewModel itself exceeds 900 lines, two neighbouring files never got the same treatment, and the file has already started growing again. The lesson is not that I solved the problem, but that I gave myself the means to see it come back.

## What I learned from it

That leading a project for a real client changes the nature of the requirement: an error in an amount is not a bug like any other, and the discipline of tests, audits and documentation stops being a box to tick and becomes the condition for a financial controller to trust the tool. That documenting for a team of five people of uneven levels is a job in its own right: a teaching-oriented onboarding guide and a glossary for developers coming from the web, who look for routes where there are ViewModels, are not a nicety: they determine who can actually contribute.

That my Git discipline was built over the course of the project rather than existing from the first commit: the first weeks carry vague messages and commits that touch several subjects at once, the later ones prefixes tied to a specific ticket. It is not just a change of vocabulary: it is what makes a history readable by someone other than yourself.

What I would do differently: settle the contract of the Excel export against the real need before writing the first 900 lines, rather than having to rethink it once the problem of overwritten formulas was noticed. Deal with a defect flagged by an internal audit the same day rather than letting it resurface in the next audit. And split my work into more targeted tasks rather than moving forward on several fronts at once, to meet deadlines more easily.

## In figures

- 5 students in the team, 393 commits in total, of which about 150 (38%) are mine
- about 26,500 lines of C# and XAML, plus auxiliary Python scripts, in the project's most advanced state
- 117 documented tests (54 on extraction, 63 on mapping), 131 out of 131 after the rework of the Excel export
- 13 PlantUML diagrams, about twenty technical documents (architecture per layer, onboarding, audits, client file)
- 3 versions delivered as signed MSIX, from January to May 2026

- No online demo: Windows desktop application for internal use, with no web version.
- Documentation: technical file delivered to the client in February 2026, kept with about twenty architecture and audit documents in the project's repository.
